summary: This tutorial explains confit, the French technique of slow-cooking food in fat, and draws on guidance from Chef Étienne Rousseau and historian Dr. Alicia Ramirez. It covers fat selection, curing, low-and-slow cooking temperatures, post-cooking maturation, versatile uses, modern variations and home-cooking tips. It also stresses that confit began as a preservation method and now applies to meats, vegetables and fruits.
one_line: A professional tutorial on confit covering fat choice, curing, low-temperature cooking, maturation, modern variations and home tips, featuring Chef Étienne Rousseau.
key_facts: Confit comes from the French word 'confire', meaning 'to preserve', and involves slow-cooking an ingredient in fat.
Confit is traditionally associated with duck legs that are cured and then slowly cooked in their own rendered fat.
For poultry such as duck or goose, chefs typically use the animal's own fat; pork confit may use lard, and olive oil suits vegetables like garlic and tomatoes.
On November 12, 2023, a panel of chefs at the Regional Cuisine Symposium affirmed that fat quality directly affects the taste and preservation properties of confit.
Curing uses a mixture of salt, herbs and spices, which seasons the meat and reduces moisture, concentrating flavor.
Dr. Alicia Ramirez's research, published after the Food Heritage Conference in September 2023, traces confit's origins to preservation needs before refrigeration.
Chef Étienne Rousseau recommends curing duck legs in the refrigerator with salt, thyme, rosemary and garlic for up to 36 hours.
At a December 15, 2023 workshop, Rousseau demonstrated cooking temperatures from 200°F (93°C) to 275°F (135°C), with about 225°F (107°C) ideal for duck confit.
Duck confit cooks for about 2 to 3 hours until the meat is practically falling off the bone.
In a January 5, 2024 column, Rousseau advised letting confit rest in the cooking fat in a cool place for at least one week before use.
Garlic confit becomes spreadable, caramelized cloves, and confited citrus has its tartness mellowed for desserts or savory dishes.
At the International Chefs Congress on February 22, 2024, Chef Jasmine Li showcased 'confit fusion' techniques, including olive oil-confit fish and pairing confit with sous vide.
Home cooks are advised to start with simpler ingredients like garlic or tomatoes and to use a heavy-bottomed pot or slow cooker, a skimming spoon and tightly sealing storage containers.
